title: Reflexive and reciprocal pronouns; numerals

objectives.can: Recognise ἑαυτοῦ, ἐμαυτοῦ, σεαυτοῦ and ἀλλήλων, and the declined numerals εἷς, δύο, τρεῖς, τέσσαρες.

explanation.summary: Greek has one pronoun for 'myself, yourself, himself' and another for 'one another'. Neither has a nominative, because neither can be the subject. The numerals 'one', 'two', 'three' and 'four' decline; most higher numerals do not.

sections.heading: Reflexive pronouns: ἐμαυτοῦ, σεαυτοῦ, ἑαυτοῦ
body: A reflexive pronoun points back to the subject of its clause: 'I deceive myself', 'you know yourself', 'he has life in himself'. There are three singular headwords, one for each person: ἐμαυτοῦ (myself), σεαυτοῦ (yourself) and ἑαυτοῦ (himself, herself, itself). They are built from the personal pronoun and αὐτός, and their endings are like those of αὐτός.

None has a nominative form, since a word that refers back to the subject cannot be the subject. Only masculine forms of the first two occur in the New Testament text analysed here. ἑαυτοῦ has masculine, feminine and neuter forms.

sections.heading: The plural of ἑαυτοῦ does all the work
body: There are no separate plural forms for 'ourselves' and 'yourselves'. The plural of ἑαυτοῦ is used for all three persons. In 1 John 1:8, ἑαυτοὺς πλανῶμεν means 'we deceive ourselves': the verb shows the person, and ἑαυτούς, accusative plural, shows that the object is the same as the subject.
Usually a reflexive refers to the subject of the clause it stands in. Occasionally, inside a subordinate phrase, it refers to the subject of the main sentence; the context shows which.

sections.heading: The reciprocal pronoun ἀλλήλων
body: ἀλλήλων means 'one another', 'each other'. It has no singular and no nominative, and nearly all its forms in the New Testament are masculine. The three case forms are the genitive ἀλλήλων, the dative ἀλλήλοις and the accusative ἀλλήλους. It is formed from ἄλλος ('other') doubled.
John 13:34 has ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, 'love one another'. In 1 John 1:7, μετ’ ἀλλήλων is 'with one another': the genitive after the preposition μετά.

sections.heading: Numerals: εἷς, δύο, τρεῖς, τέσσαρες
body: εἷς 'one' has three genders in the singular: masculine εἷς, feminine μία, neuter ἕν. The stem is ἑν- in the masculine and neuter oblique cases (ἑνός, ἑνί, ἕνα) and μι- in the feminine (μιᾶς, μιᾷ, μίαν). It agrees with its noun in gender and case. In John 10:30 the neuter ἕν is the form used, as the predicate of ἐσμεν. What that oneness consists of is a question for interpretation, not for grammar.

δύο 'two' is usually the same in every case and gender, as in Matthew 18:16, where both the accusative ἢ δύο and the genitive δύο μαρτύρων occur. A dative δυσί or δυσίν is sometimes found. τρεῖς 'three' and τέσσαρες 'four' decline, with the genitive τριῶν and τεσσάρων and the dative plural τρισίν and τέσσαρσιν; the neuter is τρία and τέσσαρα.

The cardinals above four, like πέντε, ἑπτά and δώδεκα, are generally not declined: one form serves every case and gender, and the noun shows the case. The hundreds and the thousands are an exception and behave like adjectives.

sections.heading: οὐδείς and μηδείς
body: οὐδείς and μηδείς, 'no one', 'nothing', are εἷς with a negative in front (οὐδέ, μηδέ + εἷς), and decline like it: οὐδείς, οὐδεμία, οὐδέν, genitive οὐδενός. In Greek, a second negative does not cancel the first; it strengthens it. In 1 John 1:5, σκοτία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδεμία is 'there is no darkness in him at all'. John 5:30 has οὐ δύναμαι … οὐδέν: 'I can do nothing'.

misunderstandings: Confusing ἑαυτόν (himself, reflexive) with αὐτόν (him). The reflexive points back to the subject; the personal pronoun usually points to someone else. Read ἑαυτούς πλανῶμεν as 'we deceive ourselves', not 'we deceive them'.
Looking for a nominative of the reflexive or reciprocal. There is none.
Treating δύο as a plural noun. It is a numeral, and the noun that follows has its own case. It does not decline like a noun.
Reading οὐκ … οὐδείς as 'not … no one' with the English cancelling. In Greek the negatives add up to a stronger denial.

deeper.heading: Contracted spellings
body: ἑαυτοῦ has a shorter variant with a rough breathing on the first vowel: αὑτοῦ, αὑτόν. It is easy to take for the personal pronoun αὐτοῦ, αὐτόν, which has a smooth breathing. The two are different words. Editions are not always agreed on where a reflexive stands, so the sense of the clause is the final guide.

examples.analysis: ἑαυτούς is accusative plural masculine and the object of πλανῶμεν. Its reference is the subject of the verb, ἡμεῖς, 'we', which is not written but is shown by the ending of the verb: 'we deceive ourselves'. The plural of ἑαυτοῦ serves for the first person here.

examples.analysis: ἐμαυτοῦ is genitive singular, after ἀπό: 'from myself'. It is the first-person reflexive and it looks back to the speaker. οὐδέν is the neuter of οὐδείς, accusative, the object of ποιεῖν; with the earlier Οὐ it makes a double negative that strengthens the denial: 'I can do nothing'.

options: As a double negative that makes 'there is some darkness'
As a strengthened denial: there is no darkness at all
check.explain: In Greek a second negative reinforces the first. οὐδεμία is the feminine of οὐδείς, nominative singular, agreeing with σκοτία.

reading.why: ἑαυτούς, ἀλλήλων and οὐδεμία all appear within six verses, in a short passage with very little else that is new.
